newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks end mixed ahead of July jobs data.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks end mixed ahead of July jobs data.

text.p: Stocks put in a mixed performance on Thursday, with investors turning cautious ahead of a potentially market-moving report on U.S. employment in July.
The Dow Jones industrial average snapped a streak of three consecutive record closing highs, ending down 32.28 points at 8,222.61.
But the broader market was firm. Continued strength in market-leading computer and financial stocks pushed the Standard & Poor's index of 500 stocks and the Nasdaq composite index to fresh highs.
The S&P 500 rose 2.00 points to 954.29 and the Nasdaq composite finished up 5.76 to 1,593.81.
On the New York Stock Exchange, advancing issues outnumbered declines by a ratio of 1,716 to 1,145 on volume of 547.8 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
Market players linked the Dow's drop to profit-taking by investors wary of the release on Friday of the July U.S. payrolls, wages and employment report ahead of the stock market opening.
"I think the lack of enthusiasm is because of waiting for tomorrow morning's release," said Robert Stovall, president of Stovall/Twenty-First Advisers.

Economists expect, on average, for the report to show the economy created 193,000 new jobs in July, compared with 217,000 in June. The unemployment rate is expected to dip to 4.9 percent from 5.0 percent in June.
The market will also get the July report from the National Association of Purchasing Management on Friday.

Stronger-than-expected data could derail the rally in stocks and bonds by raising inflation fears. But some analysts said the recent wave of economic news showing mild growth and subdued inflation reduces the chances the market will be blindsided by the reports.

"These things weigh a lot less on our minds now that there's such a preponderance of evidence that the economy's growing at a strong rate without inflation pressure," said Robert Robbins, market strategist at Robinson-Humphrey Co.

On Thursday the government reported that the gross domestic product expanded at a 2.2 percent annual rate in the April-June second quarter, less than half the revised 4.9 percent pace in the first quarter.
A key inflation measure in the GDP report -- the implicit price deflator -- edged up 1.4 percent in the second quarter after a 2.4 percent first-quarter rise.

The inflation-sensitive bond market extended its rally, with the 30-year Treasury up 12/32, reducing its yield to 6.30 percent from Wednesday's 6.33 percent. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.

Interest-rate senstive stocks, including banks and brokerages, were among strong performers. Chase Manhattan Corp. rose 1-1/16 to 113-9/16 and Morgan Stanley Dean Witter Discover & Co. gained 2-9/16 to 52-5/16.

Some traders said they saw investors shifting to stocks that can produce consistent earnings in a slowing economy, such as drug makers. Schering-Plough Corp. rose 3-1/16 to 54-9/16 and Campbell Soup Co. added 3/16 to 51-14/16.

"I'm seeing some profit-taking, moving away from the real growth stocks and into more defensive issues," said Frank Calta, managing director of institutional trading at Dain Bosworth. "It will be interesting to see if this pattern continues over the next couple of weeks."

Personal computer stocks extended their strong performance. Dell Computer Corp. rose 3-1/4 to 85-1/2 after Morgan Stanley Dean Witter raised its 1997 and 1998 earnings estimates on Dell. Compaq Computer Corp. gained 2-1/8 to 57-1/8 and Hewlett-Packard Co. added 2-3/16 to 70.

Student Loan Marketing Association, known as Sallie Mae, ended up 4-13/16 at 149-15/16 after shareholders voted to privatise the government-sponsored enterprise through a plan put forward by a dissident group.

Fast-food chain Wendy's International Inc. fell 2-13/16 to 24-1/2. Analysts at Smith Barney and Merrill Lynch downgraded the stock after the company reported quarterly earnings and said its second-half sales comparisons will be harder amid rising labour and raw material costs, and a higher tax rate.
The NYSE composite index rose 0.93 to 494.50, a record. The average price per share was up 9 cents.
The American Stock Exchange index added 0.98 point to an all-time high of 646.30.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues, also known as the Wilshire 5,000 -- ended at a record 9,031.428, up 24.065, or 0.27 percent.
